SMTO-EXE-0037 — SMTO couldn't understand an option in this command

GUID: 9e25cc25-bc37-4839-ac50-d30b223598c8
Slug: shell-option-unsupported
Domain: EXE · Subsystem: exe

What happened

  • The command used an unusual setting before its main action, so SMTO couldn't work out what the command would change. SMTO treats it as unknown and may refuse it or ask you first.

How to fix — simple steps

  1. Open the step and look at the command. Note the option that comes right after the program name, such as git or docker. That option is the part SMTO couldn't recognize.
  2. In the conversation, ask SMTO to run the same command without that option, or written in a more common way that does the same thing. SMTO needs a form it understands to judge whether the command only reads or also changes things.
  3. If SMTO asks you to approve the command, read it first, and approve only if you understand what it will do. SMTO couldn't check this command itself, so your approval is the safety check.

What success looks like

  • The command runs, or SMTO shows you an approval request you can understand.

If it still fails

  • Select Copy error details and send them, with the conversation name, to the person who manages SMTO. Don't loosen your permission settings to let unrecognized commands through.

Technical details

Observed condition

  • Command-family parsing (git, docker, kubectl, npm, gh, aws, gcloud and similar) met a global option before the subcommand that is not on its allowlist, so the command's effect could not be classified.

What this means

  • Command-family parsing encountered a global option it could not interpret under its conservative option allowlist, so it could not prove the underlying operation semantics. Execution, resource reconciliation and retries remain owned by the existing control flow. Use retained per-operation facts to distinguish this request from earlier effects; this explanation performs no additional work.

Why this can happen

  • Command-family parsing encountered a global option it could not interpret under its conservative option allowlist, so it could not prove the underlying operation semantics.

How to diagnose it

  • Inspect the specific command family and global option placement against the supported contract; preserve exact target and privilege scope.

How to fix it

  • Rewrite the command so any global options before the subcommand are among those recognized by agent_runtime.execution.shell_operations.operation_argv (for example git -C, docker --context, kubectl --namespace, aws --profile), or remove the unsupported option. Keep the same target and privilege; do not bypass the classifier or treat the unclassified command as a read.
  • Use a supported option from the current tool contract. Preserve the intended target and privilege scope.

Retry and execution caution

  • Correct the recorded cause, then inspect current state and existing receipts before requesting another attempt.

How to verify the fix

  • The intended command form can be classified under the current supported parser without bypassing policy.

What not to do

  • Do not bypass the unsupported-feature check or reinterpret an unsupported response as success.

Technical notes

  • Execution, resource reconciliation and retries remain owned by the existing control flow. Use retained per-operation facts to distinguish this request from earlier effects; this explanation performs no additional work.
  • Preserve the occurrence ID and safe request/operation references. Receipts and occurrence facts establish what started or completed; the catalog does not authorize retries or establish execution outcome.
